title: Quantum Enhancement Of Information-mediated Energy Transfer
authors: Shotaro Oki, Yuki Kadono, Kaito Tojo, Takahiro Sagawa, Ken Funo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermodynamics of information identifies information flow as a thermodynamic resource, but whether quantum coherence and collective coupling can enhance it at low entropy-production cost remains unresolved. We address this question for interacting open quantum systems by deriving a thermodynamic uncertainty relation that bounds information flow by entropy production in nonequilibrium steady states. We construct a quantum engine in which N-fold degenerate ground and excited states are collectively coupled to heat baths. Collective jumps enhance heat currents and information flow linearly with N, while entropy production remains independent of N, realizing a high-power, low-dissipation autonomous quantum Maxwell's demon that leverages collectively enhanced information flow to pump heat against a temperature gradient. Beyond steady states, collective interactions amplify the unitary component of quantum information flow, yielding a quadratic enhancement of the free-energy charging power of quantum batteries. Our results reveal scalable advantages of quantum coherence and collective effects in quantum engines.
tldr: Collective quantum effects enhance information flow and power in a quantum Maxwell's demon and battery with minimal entropy production.
motivation: To determine whether quantum coherence and collective coupling can enhance information-mediated energy transfer without incurring high entropy production costs.
method: Derives a thermodynamic uncertainty relation for information flow in nonequilibrium steady states, then constructs an N-fold degenerate quantum engine with collective coupling to heat baths.
result: Collective jumps linearly enhance heat currents and information flow with N while entropy production remains N-independent, and quadratic enhancement of free-energy charging power is achieved in quantum batteries.
conclusion: Quantum coherence and collective effects provide scalable advantages for high-power, low-dissipation quantum engines and batteries.

title: Industry-ready Spin-photon Interfaces For Hybrid Photonic Quantum Computing
authors: H\^elio Huet, Hubert Lam, Thibaut Pollet, Petr Steindl, Alice Bernard, Albert Adiyatullin, Petr Stepanov, William Hease, Victor Guilloux, Nico Margaria, Joris Verstraten, Raksha Singla, Samuel T. Laverick, Thinhinane Bennour, Tomas Alexandre de Sousa, Davide Stefani, Mathias Pont, Maxime Descampeaux, Bianca Scaparra, Martin A. Jacobsen, Klaus D. J\"ons, Rinaldo Trotta, Aristide Lema\^itre, Martina Morassi, Olivier Krebs, Lo\"ic Lanco, Niels Gregersen, Alexia Auff\`eves, Maria Maffei, Shane Mansfield, Jean Senellart, Thomas Volz, Viviana Villafa\~ne, Stephen C. abstract: ArXiv:2606.27787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid photonic quantum computers, combining stationary matter qubits and flying photonic qubits, offer an intrinsically networked and resource-efficient route to large-scale, error-corrected quantum computation. Their core components are cavity-coupled matter qubits that act as light--matter interfaces, enabling: high-efficiency on-demand single-photon generation, stable near-unity photon indistinguishability and spin--multi-photon entanglement. Semiconductor quantum dots in microcavities are a leading platform for realizing such devices. Yet reaching the performance, reproducibility and spin-coherence thresholds for large-scale error correction remains a major challenge requiring industrial fabrication and control. Here we report thousands of monolithic semiconductor quantum-dot devices fabricated using a III--V pilot production-line process compatible with large-scale deployment. Systematic control of source parameters yields state-of-the-art efficiency and supports a path to optical losses below fault-tolerance thresholds. Using field-quadrature state reconstruction as a stringent joint test of efficiency and indistinguishability, we observe near-unity photon quantum purity stable over tens of minutes and a record single-photon Wigner-function negativity. We further demonstrate seven-partite spin--multi-photon entanglement and spin coherence extendable to microsecond timescales in the low-magnetic-field regime. Finally, photons from distant sources are as indistinguishable as photons emitted successively by a single source. These results establish foundry-compatible III--V quantum dots as a scalable platform for hybrid photonic quantum computing.
tldr: Demonstrates industry-fabricated quantum dot microcavity devices achieving state-of-the-art single-photon purity, indistinguishability, and spin-multi-photon entanglement for hybrid photonic quantum computing.
motivation: Scalable, high-performance spin-photon interfaces are needed for hybrid photonic quantum computers, but current devices lack reproducibility and coherence for fault-tolerant operation.
method: Thousands of monolithic semiconductor quantum-dot devices were fabricated using a III-V pilot production line, characterized via field-quadrature state reconstruction and spin-photon entanglement experiments.
result: Achieved near-unity photon quantum purity, record Wigner-function negativity, seven-partite spin-multi-photon entanglement, and microsecond spin coherence; photons from distant sources are as indistinguishable as from a single source.
conclusion: Foundry-compatible III-V quantum dots are a scalable platform for hybrid photonic quantum computing, meeting key thresholds for error correction.

title: Reservoir-independent Lossless Charging And Protected Storage Of An Open Quantum Battery
authors: Asad Ali, H. Kuniyil, M. I Hussain, M. T Rahim, Saif Al-Kuwari, James Q. Quach
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A quantum battery charged through a lossy intermediate state faces a structural trade-off between charging speed and dissipation. We show that an exact algebraic cancellation removes it in a driven three-level cell: the radiatively decaying state is fed by a single bright amplitude, and a counterdiabatic field annuls the lone residual source that drives it, holding the lossy state identically empty. Charging is then lossless -- not one photon is emitted through the bridge -- at any one-photon detuning, coupling, linewidth, and speed down to the rotating-wave limit, with no adiabatic elimination, so the charging power is bounded by the drive amplitude (a quantum speed limit) rather than by dissipation. Crucially, this losslessness is independent of the reservoir: because the dark sector never engages the system-bath coupling, the emission vanishes exactly for an arbitrary spectral density, Markovian or not, as an exact damped-pseudomode treatment confirms to machine precision across all memory times. The entire non-Hermitian structure -- a Markovian second-order exceptional point that reservoir memory promotes to a third-order one, and the attendant dissipation phase diagram -- lives in the bright sector, from which the protocol is by construction exempt. This inverts dissipation-engineered charging, where an exceptional point or reservoir memory is a resource; here the lossy sector is never populated at all. The same dark-state structure protects the stored charge, converting fast radiative self-discharge into the slow metastable lifetime, with residuals quadratic in the control error. We detail experimental requirements and representative parameters for neutral alkaline-earth atoms, trapped ions, transmons, and defect centers.
tldr: A protocol for lossless charging and protected storage of a quantum battery using dark-state engineering, independent of reservoir properties.
motivation: Quantum batteries suffer from a trade-off between charging speed and dissipation when charged through a lossy intermediate state; the authors aim to eliminate this trade-off.
method: They use a driven three-level system where a counterdiabatic field cancels the residual source driving the lossy state, keeping it identically empty, and analyze the non-Hermitian structure.
result: Charging becomes lossless at any detuning, coupling, linewidth, and speed, with power bounded only by the drive amplitude; the dark state also protects stored charge from fast radiative decay.
conclusion: The protocol achieves reservoir-independent lossless charging and protected storage, with experimental feasibility in various platforms.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper presents a protocol for lossless charging of a quantum battery using a driven three-level system. The key idea is to exploit a dark-state mechanism where a radiatively decaying intermediate state is never populated, despite being coupled to the drive and the reservoir. The authors show that by applying a counterdiabatic field, the lone residual source driving the lossy state is annulled, resulting in zero emission through that state. This holds for any one-photon detuning, coupling strength, linewidth, and speed, down to the rotating-wave limit, without requiring adiabatic elimination. The charging power is thus bounded only by the drive amplitude (a quantum speed limit) rather than by dissipation. Crucially, the losslessness is independent of the reservoir's spectral density, whether Markovian or non-Markovian, as confirmed by an exact damped-pseudomode treatment. The non-Hermitian structure of the system features a Markovian second-order exceptional point that becomes third-order with reservoir memory, but the protocol operates in the dark sector, avoiding dissipation entirely. The stored charge is protected by the same dark-state structure, converting fast radiative self-discharge into a slow metastable lifetime, with residuals quadratic in control errors. Experimental requirements and representative parameters are provided for neutral alkaline-earth atoms, trapped ions, transmons, and defect centers.

Proof that losslessness holds for arbitrary reservoir spectral density (Markovian or non-Markovian) and is independent of system parameters such as detuning, coupling, and linewidth.
Identification of a structural trade-off between charging speed and dissipation, and its complete cancellation via counterdiabatic driving.
Characterization of the non-Hermitian structure (exceptional points) in the bright sector, showing that the protocol avoids dissipation entirely by operating in the dark sector.
Experimental feasibility analysis with concrete parameters for four different physical platforms: neutral alkaline-earth atoms, trapped ions, transmons, and defect centers.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. They start with a driven three-level system in a ladder configuration, where the intermediate state is radiatively coupled to a reservoir. Using a master equation approach, they derive conditions for the dark state where the intermediate state remains empty. They introduce a counterdiabatic field to cancel the residual driving of the lossy state. The analysis is performed without adiabatic elimination, ensuring exactness. To verify reservoir independence, they use an exact damped-pseudomode treatment that captures non-Markovian effects by discretizing the reservoir into pseudomodes. This allows them to simulate the dynamics for various memory times and confirm zero emission to machine precision. The non-Hermitian structure is analyzed by examining the eigenvalues of the Liouvillian superoperator, revealing exceptional points of order two and three. The analysis is rigorous and combines algebraic cancellations with numerical verification.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that the charging process is lossless: not a single photon is emitted through the intermediate state. This is shown to hold for any one-photon detuning, coupling strength, linewidth, and speed, down to the rotating-wave limit. The charging power is bounded by the drive amplitude, i.e., a quantum speed limit, rather than by dissipation. The losslessness is independent of the reservoir's spectral density; the damped-pseudomode treatment confirms zero emission for all memory times. The non-Hermitian analysis reveals a Markovian second-order exceptional point that becomes third-order with reservoir memory, but the protocol operates in the dark sector, so dissipation is avoided. The stored charge's self-discharge rate is reduced from the fast radiative rate to a slow metastable lifetime, with residuals scaling quadratically in control errors. Experimental parameters are given: for example, in neutral alkaline-earth atoms, the intermediate state linewidth is ~10 MHz, and the drive Rabi frequency can be ~1 MHz, yielding charging times ~1 μs with negligible emission.

title: Jarzynski Equality For Counterwork Under Reversed Memory-filtered Driving
authors: Pierre Naz\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a counterwork functional generated by a sign-inverting memory-filtered effective protocol. Given an imposed protocol [MATH], the effective protocol [MATH] is obtained by applying an active protocol-memory kernel to [MATH], rather than by invoking a passive bath response. The counterwork is then the ordinary Hamiltonian work associated with [MATH], so that Jarzynski's equality applies directly to it. When [MATH] reverses the endpoints of [MATH], the corresponding free-energy difference satisfies [MATH], and the exponential average of the counterwork is the reciprocal of that of the original work. We derive the kernel normalization realizing this reversed displacement and show, by Jensen's inequality, that the product of the exponentials of the average work and counterwork is bounded by unity, implying [MATH]. Thus negative average counterwork is possible only when compensated by the average work of the original operation. We further discuss the counteroperation under incomplete thermodynamic information, showing that the robust strategy is to enforce endpoint reversal while minimizing dissipated counterwork.
tldr: Introduces a counterwork functional for memory-filtered driving that satisfies Jarzynski's equality, enabling a reciprocal relation between work and counterwork averages.
motivation: Extend fluctuation theorems to non-Markovian driving protocols where the effective protocol is generated by a memory kernel rather than passive bath response.
method: Defines a counterwork as the Hamiltonian work under a sign-inverted memory-filtered effective protocol; derives kernel normalization for endpoint reversal and uses Jensen's inequality to bound the product of exponential averages.
result: The exponential average of counterwork equals the reciprocal of that of the original work when endpoints are reversed; negative average counterwork requires compensation by positive average work.
conclusion: Provides a framework for analyzing work relations under incomplete thermodynamic information, with optimal strategy being endpoint reversal while minimizing dissipated counterwork.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces the concept of a 'counterwork functional' generated by a sign-inverting memory-filtered effective protocol. The authors propose an active protocol-memory kernel applied to the time derivative of an imposed protocol λ(t) to produce an effective protocol Λ(t), as opposed to traditional passive bath response. The counterwork is defined as the ordinary Hamiltonian work associated with H(Γ, Λ(t)), allowing Jarzynski's equality to apply directly. When Λ(t) reverses the endpoints of λ(t), the free-energy difference satisfies ΔF_C = -ΔF_W, and the exponential average of the counterwork equals the reciprocal of that of the original work. The kernel normalization for reversed displacement is derived, and Jensen's inequality yields that the product of exponentials of average work and counterwork is bounded by unity, implying ⟨C⟩ + ⟨W⟩ ≥ 0. Thus, negative average counterwork is possible only if compensated by positive average work. The paper also discusses counteroperation under incomplete thermodynamic information, advocating for endpoint reversal while minimizing dissipated counterwork.

Derivation of kernel normalization that achieves reversed endpoint displacement.
Proof that the exponential average of counterwork is the reciprocal of that of the original work when endpoints are reversed.
Establishment of the inequality ⟨C⟩ + ⟨W⟩ ≥ 0 via Jensen's inequality, linking average work and counterwork.
Discussion of robust strategies for counteroperation under incomplete thermodynamic information.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is theoretical and analytical, rooted in stochastic thermodynamics and fluctuation theorems. The authors define an effective protocol Λ(t) by applying an active memory kernel to the derivative of the imposed protocol λ(t), contrasting with passive bath response. They then compute the counterwork as the Hamiltonian work for the system evolving under Λ(t). Using Jarzynski's equality, they relate the exponential average of counterwork to the free-energy difference ΔF_C. By imposing endpoint reversal (Λ(τ) = λ(0) and Λ(0) = λ(τ)), they derive the necessary kernel normalization. Jensen's inequality is applied to bound the product of exponential averages. The analysis extends to scenarios with incomplete information, where the kernel is optimized to minimize dissipated counterwork while ensuring endpoint reversal.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key result is that when the effective protocol reverses the endpoints of the original protocol, the free-energy difference satisfies ΔF_C = -ΔF_W, leading to ⟨e^{-βC}⟩ = e^{-βΔF_C} = e^{βΔF_W} = 1/⟨e^{-βW}⟩. From Jensen's inequality, the authors obtain ⟨e^{-βC}⟩ ≥ e^{-β⟨C⟩} and similarly for W, yielding e^{-β(⟨C⟩+⟨W⟩)} ≤ 1, so ⟨C⟩ + ⟨W⟩ ≥ 0. This implies that negative average counterwork is possible only if the average work is positive and at least as large in magnitude. The paper does not provide numerical values but focuses on general inequalities and exact relations. The discussion on incomplete information suggests that the optimal strategy is to enforce endpoint reversal while minimizing dissipated counterwork, though no explicit optimization is performed.

The derivation is mathematically rigorous, using well-established tools like Jarzynski's equality and Jensen's inequality.
The results are general and not tied to specific system details, enhancing their applicability.
The discussion of incomplete information provides practical guidance for experimental implementation.

The counterwork functional and the derived inequalities are relevant for understanding work fluctuations in quantum systems driven by non-Markovian or engineered protocols. The concept of endpoint reversal and the bound ⟨C⟩+⟨W⟩≥0 could have implications for quantum heat engines, information erasure, and the thermodynamics of quantum control. The paper's focus on memory kernels also ties into research on non-Markovian quantum dynamics and open quantum systems.

The derivations are clear and rigorous, and the results are elegant, particularly the reciprocal relation between exponential averages and the inequality linking average work and counterwork. However, the lack of experimental or numerical validation and the potential difficulty in realizing the sign-inverting memory kernel limit its immediate impact. The work opens up interesting avenues for further research, especially in quantum thermodynamics and control. Overall, it is a high-quality theoretical paper with moderate novelty and strong potential for future developments.

title: No Cloning Of Quantum Ensembles
authors: Zhenyu Du, Siyuan Cheng, Qi Zhao, Xiongfeng Ma, Xiao Yuan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern quantum physics now enables control of quantum systems at the level of individual trajectories, opening a new frontier that links quantum information theory, quantum many-body physics, and quantum thermodynamics, and uncovers novel non-equilibrium phenomena such as deep thermalization and measurement-induced entanglement. However, a central challenge remains: their characterization relies on measuring nonlinear properties of individual quantum states, a task tantamount to fine-grained cloning of a quantum ensemble. Here, the fundamental laws governing the cloning of quantum ensembles are investigated. First, a general no-cloning theorem for arbitrary ensembles is established from an information-theoretic perspective, even assuming multiple copies of the ensemble's purification. It is then shown that this barrier can be unexpectedly circumvented for physical ensembles generated by finite-time evolutions. Nevertheless, these tasks are proven to remain computationally intractable, even when the full circuit description of state preparation is known. This stands in sharp contrast to the conventional no-cloning theorem, which relies on the state being unknown. Together, these results establish new fundamental principles of quantum mechanics, reveal intrinsic trade-offs among sample complexity, computational complexity, and quantum measurements, and highlight the necessity of problem-specific strategies for probing measurement-induced quantum phenomena.
tldr: Establishes a general no-cloning theorem for quantum ensembles and shows that while physical ensembles can circumvent it, the task remains computationally intractable.
motivation: Characterizing nonlinear properties of quantum states in many-body systems requires fine-grained cloning of ensembles, which is believed to be impossible; this work formalizes the fundamental limits.
method: Uses information-theoretic arguments to prove a no-cloning theorem for arbitrary ensembles, then analyzes physical ensembles generated by finite-time evolutions and proves computational hardness via complexity theory.
result: Proves that cloning arbitrary ensembles is impossible even with multiple copies of the purification, but physical ensembles can be cloned; however, the cloning task is computationally intractable even with full circuit description.
conclusion: Establishes new fundamental principles linking no-cloning, sample complexity, and computational complexity, highlighting the need for problem-specific strategies in probing measurement-induced quantum phenomena.

The authors first establish a general no-cloning theorem for arbitrary ensembles from an information-theoretic perspective, showing that even with multiple copies of the ensemble's purification, perfect cloning is impossible. They then demonstrate that this barrier can be circumvented for physical ensembles generated by finite-time evolutions, but prove that such cloning tasks remain computationally intractable even when the full circuit description of state preparation is known. This contrasts with the conventional no-cloning theorem, which relies on the state being unknown. The results reveal intrinsic trade-offs among sample complexity, computational complexity, and quantum measurements, and highlight the need for problem-specific strategies in probing measurement-induced quantum phenomena.

title: Single-sideband-interference Twin-field Quantum Key Distribution Without Global Phase Locking
authors: Xingjian Li, Bingkun Wang, Jianyong Hu, Jianqiang Liu, Shuxiao Wu, Guosheng Feng, Zhixing Qiao, Changgang Yang, Ruiyun Chen, Chengbing Qin, Guofeng Zhang, Liantuan Xiao, Suotang Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Twin-field quantum key distribution (TF QKD) can overcome the fundamental rate loss limit of repeaterless quantum links, but its practical deployment has long been hindered by the requirement of global phase locking between two independent lasers. By revisiting the fundamental principles of optical interference, this work reveals that interference in TF QKD inherently relies only on the instantaneous phase alignment of two independent optical pulses at the moment they temporally overlap, rather than on continuous global phase synchronization. Guided by this insight, we propose and demonstrate a single-sideband-interference TF-QKD protocol that eliminates global phase locking. Each user employs an IQ modulator to generate a weak single sideband as the quantum signal, while the intrinsically phase-correlated optical carrier propagates as a real-time phase reference. Carrier interference at the receiver enables real-time phase extraction and feedback compensation for the sidebands. Unlike prior no phase locking approaches requiring second- or microsecond-level coherence, in principle, our scheme reduces this requirement to nanoseconds. We achieve 98% interference visibility over 100.8 km fibre and secure key rates surpassing the PLOB bound in the high-loss regime, providing a simpler route towards practical long-distance quantum communication networks.

title: Non-equilibrium Quantum Thermometry With Bosonic Samples
authors: Marek Winczewski, Micha{\l} Horodecki, Ricard Ravell Rodr\'iguez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27894v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study low-temperature non-equilibrium quantum thermometry with a bosonic probe: a quantum harmonic oscillator strongly coupled to a bosonic bath at temperature [MATH] through a Drude--Ohmic spectral density. We treat the probe--bath dynamics both exactly, using the quadratic solution of Boyanovsky and Jasnow, and within a renormalized Gorini--Kossakowski--Lindblad--Sudarshan (GKLS) master equation. From the time-dependent covariance matrix we extract the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for general single-mode Gaussian probe states, including squeezed ones. In the strong-coupling, non-Markovian regime the QFI is non-monotonic in time, displaying bath-memory revivals that make a finite interrogation time [MATH] strictly optimal. By contrast, we prove that the Markovian QFI rises monotonically to its stationary value and develops no interior optimum, so that its optimum is always pinned to the boundary [MATH]; this complements existing Markovian precision-rate bounds, which concern [MATH] rather than the single-shot QFI [MATH]. Squeezed initial states yield a large transient advantage that thermalisation eventually erases, establishing squeezing and interrogation time as complementary thermometric resources. At equilibrium, strong coupling replaces the exponential Boltzmann suppression of the low-temperature relative error by a far milder polynomial divergence. As the model maps directly onto circuit quantum electrodynamics, these protocols appear within current experimental reach.

motivation: Accurate low-temperature thermometry is crucial for quantum technologies, but standard Markovian models fail in the strong-coupling, non-Markovian regime. The authors aim to characterize the ultimate precision limits and identify optimal protocols.
method: The probe-bath dynamics are solved exactly using the quadratic solution of Boyanovsky and Jasnow and approximated with a renormalized GKLS master equation. The quantum Fisher information is extracted from the time-dependent covariance matrix for general single-mode Gaussian states.

Squeezed initial states provide transient advantages, and strong coupling replaces exponential Boltzmann suppression with polynomial divergence at low temperatures.
conclusion: The work establishes squeezing and interrogation time as complementary resources for quantum thermometry, and the protocols are experimentally feasible in circuit QED platforms.

title: A Quantum Method Of Types
authors: Arick Grootveld
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The method of types is a fundamental tool in classical information theory, with applications ranging from composite hypothesis testing and universal source coding to the capacity of arbitrarily varying channels. In this work we introduce an empirical operator acting as a quantum analog of the empirical distribution. We show that this empirical operator satisfies combinatorial and large-deviation bounds, which in combination describe a quantum method of types. As an application, we use this quantum method of types to prove a universal achievability result for composite quantum hypothesis testing.

title: Engineering Of non-Hermitian Interactions In Digital Qudit Quantum Simulators
authors: Matteo M. Wauters, Paolo Boschetto, Edoardo Ballini, Alberto Biella, Philipp Hauke
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-Hermitian Hamiltonians are a fascinating class of many-body models that describe the effective dynamics of quantum systems interacting with the environment through particle, energy, or information exchange. Although their theoretical framework is well established, the controlled engineering of such Hamiltonians in the context of quantum simulations remains challenging, even more so when the non-Hermitian part describes a [MATH]-body interaction. Qudit quantum simulators offer a compelling framework to implement such models. We theoretically investigate the dynamics of a one-dimensional chain of qudits undergoing hybrid unitary-projective evolution, where suitably designed measurements constrain the dynamics to a Zeno subspace. As we illustrate for the case of qutrits, within the Zeno subspace the dynamics is governed by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian for an ensemble of pseudo-spins [MATH], which can inherit non-Hermitian two-body interactions with the same connectivity as the full qutrit chain. We derive an analytical relation linking the monitored qutrits' evolution to a desired target non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and validate the effective description through numerical simulations of a representative model. Our scheme provides a constructive route for the realization of a large class of interacting non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians in experimentally relevant multilevel quantum platforms, including trapped ions and superconducting circuits.

conclusion: The scheme provides a constructive route to realize a large class of interacting non-Hermitian many-body Hamiltonians in multilevel quantum platforms like trapped ions and superconducting circuits.

title: Scalable Acceleration Of Many-Body Quantum Dynamics Via Time-Rescaling
authors: Edson B. de Almeida Filho, \^angelo F. Da Silva Fran\c{c}a, Bert\'ulio de Lima Bernardo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27630v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fast quantum control is essential to overcome decoherence in contemporary quantum platforms, yet achieving this in many-body systems remains a major challenge. We show that the time-rescaling (TR) method enables efficient acceleration of closed many-body quantum dynamics, extending its applicability beyond previously studied regimes. Applying TR to the transverse-field Ising model with a longitudinal field, we demonstrate a significant enhancement of quantum annealing performance, maintaining high ground-state fidelity at evolution times where standard adiabatic dynamics breaks down, with only weak dependence on system size. We further demonstrate high-fidelity preparation of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states in many-body systems, where TR extends the accessible system sizes within fixed evolution times. We additionally show that the Mandelstam-Tamm quantum speed limit does not fundamentally limit the acceleration achievable through TR, as the reduction in evolution time is exactly compensated by increased energy fluctuations. These results establish TR as a scalable and experimentally viable approach to fast quantum control in many-body systems.
tldr: The time-rescaling method accelerates many-body quantum dynamics, enhancing quantum annealing and GHZ state preparation while circumventing the Mandelstam-Tamm speed limit.
motivation: Fast quantum control is needed to overcome decoherence, but accelerating many-body dynamics is challenging. The paper aims to extend the time-rescaling method to many-body systems.
method: The authors apply time-rescaling to the transverse-field Ising model with a longitudinal field, demonstrating acceleration of quantum annealing and GHZ state preparation. They analyze the Mandelstam-Tamm bound in the context of TR.
result: Time-rescaling significantly improves ground-state fidelity in quantum annealing with weak system-size dependence, enables high-fidelity GHZ state preparation for larger systems, and shows that the quantum speed limit does not fundamentally restrict TR acceleration.
conclusion: Time-rescaling is a scalable and experimentally viable approach for fast quantum control in many-body systems, with implications for quantum thermodynamics and speed limits.

title: Memory And Thermal Amplification In Spin--cavity Squared Commutators
authors: Yong-Hong Ma, Hui-Hui Xu, Jian-Zhuang Wu, Quan-Zhen Ding, Wu-Ming Liu, Xin-Yu Zhao, E Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27648v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Squared commutators in the Holstein--Primakoff limit of a spin--cavity system provide a compact way to separate propagation from covariance growth in a finite-temperature reservoir with memory. In the finite-temperature NMQSD construction, the linear quadrature commutator is fixed by the retarded spin--cavity propagator, whereas a quadratic commutator carries the same retarded factor together with a covariance factor. For a zero-mean Gaussian state, \(C_{R_i^2,R_j}(t)=4|\kappa_{ij}(t)|^2V_{ii}(t)\); the symmetrized expression gives the spin-side and mixed channels. Since \(\bar n\) enters the covariance sector but not the homogeneous retarded kernel, raising \(\bar n\) from 0 to 1 leaves the linear transfer unchanged while increasing the quadratic signal. Varying the bath-memory rate and the counter-rotating coupling within the stable HP region then shows how stored cavity history changes both the transfer weight and its distribution in time. The calculation separates memory-dependent propagation from thermal covariance growth in collective spin--cavity dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies memory and thermal amplification in a spin-cavity system using squared commutators, separating propagation from covariance growth in a finite-temperature reservoir.
motivation: Understanding how memory and temperature affect quantum dynamics in hybrid spin-cavity systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.
method: The authors use the Holstein-Primakoff approximation and the NMQSD approach to derive linear and quadratic commutators, analyzing how bath memory and counter-rotating coupling influence transfer weights.
result: They find that increasing the thermal photon number enhances the quadratic signal without affecting linear transfer, and that memory-dependent propagation can be separated from thermal covariance growth.
conclusion: The work provides a framework to analyze memory and thermal effects in collective spin-cavity dynamics, relevant for quantum thermodynamics and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Rare Events Govern Defect Formation Under Weak Symmetry Breaking
authors: Jiang Liu, Peng Yang, Matteo Baggioli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crossing a continuous phase transition out of equilibrium typically generates topological defects whose density obeys a universal power-law scaling predicted by the Kibble-Zurek mechanism. Recent numerical studies have revealed systematic deviations from this scaling in the presence of weak explicit symmetry breaking, manifested as an additional exponential suppression of defect formation. However, the origin of this correction and a general theoretical framework to describe it have remained elusive. Here, using large-deviation theory, we show that defect formation under weak symmetry breaking is controlled by rare fluctuations that drive local regions into the disfavored symmetry-broken state. This mechanism yields a closed-form expression for the defect density in arbitrary dimensions, valid in the weak-field and weak-noise limits. These theoretical predictions are verified through direct simulations of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau models in one and two spatial dimensions.
tldr: Defect formation under weak symmetry breaking is governed by rare fluctuations, leading to an exponential suppression beyond the Kibble-Zurek scaling.
motivation: Recent numerical studies show deviations from Kibble-Zurek scaling under weak symmetry breaking, but a theoretical explanation was missing.
method: Large-deviation theory is used to analyze rare fluctuations that drive local regions into the disfavored symmetry-broken state, yielding a closed-form expression for defect density.
result: The derived expression matches simulations of stochastic Ginzburg-Landau models in 1D and 2D, confirming that rare events control defect formation.
conclusion: The work provides a general theoretical framework for defect formation under weak symmetry breaking, highlighting the role of rare fluctuations.

They show that defect formation under weak symmetry breaking is dominated by rare fluctuations that locally drive the system into the disfavored symmetry-broken state. This leads to a closed-form expression for the defect density in arbitrary dimensions, valid in the weak-field and weak-noise limits. title: Simulating The Dynamics Of Markovian Quantum Processes By Quantum Collision Models On Quantum Computers
authors: Zeqing Wang, Julian D. Teske, Anshuman Bhardwaj, Masahiro O. Takahashi, Seiji Yunoki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hamiltonian dynamics have been widely implemented on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices in recent years. In contrast, experimental demonstrations of Markovian quantum dynamics remain limited, because implementing nonunitary evolution on quantum computers is challenging. Quantum collision models provide a natural approach to this problem by coupling the system to ancillas to realize dissipation. However, previous implementations of quantum collision models on quantum computers have typically been restricted to one or two system qubits and fewer than 12 time steps, owing to noise, circuit depth, the overhead of ancilla reset, and limited qubit resources. In this work, we experimentally simulate Markovian quantum processes with local and nonlocal dissipation on both trapped-ion and superconducting quantum computers. By employing hardware-specific ancilla strategies, we realize simulations with up to seven system qubits, corresponding to 13 qubits in total, and 40 time steps. Our results demonstrate that, even for the same physical model, the optimal implementation strategy depends strongly on the hardware characteristics of the quantum computer.
tldr: This paper experimentally simulates Markovian quantum processes using quantum collision models on trapped-ion and superconducting quantum computers, scaling to 7 system qubits and 40 time steps.
motivation: Implementing nonunitary Markovian dynamics on quantum computers is challenging; quantum collision models offer a natural approach but previous implementations were limited to small systems and few time steps.
method: The authors employ hardware-specific ancilla strategies to implement quantum collision models on both trapped-ion and superconducting platforms, coupling system qubits to ancillas to realize dissipation.
result: They achieve simulations with up to 7 system qubits (13 total qubits) and 40 time steps, demonstrating that the optimal implementation strategy depends on hardware characteristics.
conclusion: The work shows that quantum collision models can be scaled to larger systems on current quantum hardware, with performance varying by platform, providing a practical route to simulating open quantum systems.

title: Squeezing Enhanced Homodyne Weak Force Sensing In Cavity Optomechanics
authors: Madan Mohan Mahana, Sanket Das, Tarak Nath Dey
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavity optomechanical systems have emerged as a promising platform for quantum sensing. Quantum mechanics imposes a standard quantum limit (SQL) on the force-sensitivity for the standard homodyne phase quadrature measurement of the cavity's output field. In this paper, we investigate ways to enhance sensitivity beyond SQL for weak-force measurement by adopting a variational homodyne quadrature readout and quantum squeezing. Our study reveals a remarkable improvement in the force sensitivity of a cavity optomechanical sensor at a suitable homodyne angle, compared with standard phase quadrature detection of the cavity output field within a specific frequency band. We show that the force sensitivity can be further improved by intra-cavity squeezing (ICS) or injected external squeezing (IES) of the cavity mode. Both variational homodyne readout and quantum squeezing induce quantum correlation between the amplitude and phase quadratures of the cavity's output field, thereby improving the force sensitivity. The squeezing-enhanced variational homodyne detection scheme can enable high-precision sensing across various hybrid quantum platforms.

motivation: Cavity optomechanical systems are promising for quantum sensing, but standard homodyne detection is limited by the SQL. The authors aim to enhance sensitivity beyond this limit using quantum squeezing and variational readout.
method: The authors theoretically analyze a cavity optomechanical sensor with intra-cavity or injected squeezing, combined with variational homodyne quadrature readout, to induce quantum correlations between amplitude and phase quadratures.
result: They show that both intra-cavity and injected squeezing significantly improve force sensitivity over a specific frequency band compared to standard phase quadrature detection.
conclusion: The squeezing-enhanced variational homodyne scheme enables high-precision sensing and can be applied across various hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Factorization Through Lorentz Cones
authors: Guillaume Aubrun, Francesca la Piana, Alexander M\"uller-Hermes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A pair of proper cones [MATH] is said to have the Lorentz factorization property (LFP) if every [MATH]-positive map factors through a direct sum of Lorentzian cones, i.e., cones over Euclidean balls. Clearly, [MATH] has the LFP if either [MATH] or [MATH] is a direct sum of Lorentzian cones, and our main goal is to find other examples. We show that such examples cannot be found for pairs [MATH] where [MATH], or in the case where both [MATH] and [MATH] are polyhedral. We also focus on the case where [MATH] is the square-based cone in [MATH]. Here, we show that [MATH] has the LFP whenever [MATH] is a symmetric cone, i.e., a direct sum of Lorentz cones, cones of positive semidefinite matrices over the real numbers, complex numbers or quaternions, and the cone of [MATH] positive semidefinite matrices over the octonions. We leave open the question whether there are more examples, but we show that this list cannot be extended by any strictly convex cone [MATH] or for a cone [MATH] with [MATH]. Finally, we discuss an application to a problem in quantum information theory.

motivation: Understanding the structure of positive maps between cones is fundamental in quantum information, particularly for entanglement theory and channel capacities. The Lorentz factorization property provides a way to simplify such maps.
method: The authors use convex geometry and cone theory to analyze when a positive map between two proper cones factors through a direct sum of Lorentzian cones. They prove impossibility results for certain cone pairs and characterize the case where one cone is the square-based cone.
result: They show that if either cone is a direct sum of Lorentzian cones, the LFP holds, and no other examples exist when the domain or codomain has dimension ≤ 3 or both cones are polyhedral. For the square-based cone, LFP holds exactly when the other cone is symmetric (direct sum of Lorentz, PSD over reals/complex/quaternions, or octonionic PSD).
conclusion: The Lorentz factorization property is largely characterized, with only a few open cases remaining. The results have implications for the structure of positive maps in quantum information, potentially aiding in entanglement detection or channel analysis.

title: Verifiable And Collusion-Resistant Multi-Party Quantum Private Set Operations
authors: Zixian Gong, Kun Tian, Yi Zhang, Fengxia Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27994v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Threshold private set intersection (TPSI) allows parties to reveal their intersection only when its cardinality reaches a prescribed threshold. Existing quantum TPSI protocols typically rely on a third party (TP) to interpret the final results, which deviates from the cardinality-testing paradigm of TPSI. In this paper, we propose a quantum multiparty TPSI protocol with explicit cardinality testing. Our protocol develops a rotation-based quantum construction in which single-photon sequences are sequentially processed through participant-side data rotations, TP--participant masking rotations, and correlated aggregate rotations. This design produces hidden-label measurement vectors: TP can complete the final measurement, but cannot interpret the semantic meaning of the outcomes. Based on these hidden measurements, we further realize the threshold decision through an oblivious linear evaluation (OLE)-based inner product procedure and a lightweight garbled circuit, revealing only \(\mathbf 1[|\bigcap_i X_i|\ge \tau]\) before conditional intersection reconstruction. We prove the correctness and security of the proposed protocol, and further validate its feasibility through quantum-circuit simulations implemented on the IBM platform.
tldr: A quantum multi-party threshold private set intersection protocol with explicit cardinality testing using rotation-based encoding and oblivious linear evaluation.
motivation: Existing quantum TPSI protocols rely on a third party to interpret results, deviating from the cardinality-testing paradigm; this work aims to provide a protocol with explicit threshold decision without revealing semantic meaning.
method: The protocol uses single-photon sequences with participant-side data rotations, TP-participant masking rotations, and correlated aggregate rotations to produce hidden-label measurement vectors, then applies OLE-based inner product and garbled circuits for threshold decision.
result: Correctness and security are proven, and feasibility is validated via quantum-circuit simulations on IBM platform.
conclusion: The proposed protocol achieves collusion-resistant and verifiable multi-party private set operations with explicit threshold testing, advancing quantum secure multi-party computation.

title: Composing Quantum Instruments
authors: Robert I. Booth, Dominik Leichtle, Alex Rice, Kim Worrall
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28291v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the composition of classically-controlled quantum instruments--the natural quantum analogue of Markov kernels. Defining this composition for quantum instruments with continuous outcomes requires an integral of quantum channel-valued functions with respect to a quantum instrument. We construct this integral in the Heisenberg picture using the Okamura-Ozawa normal extension to a von Neumann tensor product. This integral recovers the expected finite formula, preserves normal complete positivity and subunitality, and provides the multiplication for a monad governing the composition of quantum instruments. As an immediate consequence, we identify the category of quantum Markov kernels as the Kleisli category of this monad.

title: Photon Avalanche Triggered By A Single Photon In A Bistable Nonlinear Optical Cavity
authors: Asian Selvakumaran, Anna Minguzzi, Iacopo Carusotto, Maxime Richard
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We theoretically investigate the response of a coherently-driven nonlinear optical cavity to an additional incident single photon. Using a quantum description of the nonlinear dynamics that fully accounts for the quantum fluctuations of the cavity field and for the discrete nature of the incident photon, we characterize the quantum dynamics of single-photon-stimulated jumps from the low-photon-number to the high-photon-number state of the optical bistability loop. We find that the system can exhibit a giant response to this single quantum of excitation, rooted in the phase-transition picture of optical bistability. In addition to shedding light on the role of quantum fluctuations in the non-equilibrium dynamics of a nonlinear optical cavity, our results suggest a strategy for an all-optical single-photon avalanche detector.

title: Enhancing Quantum Metrology With High-order Fisher Information And Experiments
authors: Xin-Zhu Liu, Jun-Li Jiang, Yan-Han Yang, Li-Ming Zhao, Xue Yang, Shao-Ming Fei, Ming-Xing Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fisher information plays a central role in statistics and quantum metrology, providing the basis for the celebrated Cram\'{e}r-Rao bound. In this work, we introduce a new information measure based on higher-order Fisher information and show that it naturally leads to a generalized uncertainty relation for parameter estimation, which can be regarded as an extension of the Cram\'er-Rao bound. As an application, we analyze the case of quantum phase estimation with a single qubit and compare our theoretical bounds with the well-known established hierarchical bounds. Finally, we experimentally validate the proposed framework using a photonic platform.

title: Standard-quantum-limit-surpassing Vector Polarimetry Using Rydberg Atoms In An Su(1,1) Interferometer
authors: Weiqiang Guan, Yuetao Chen, Jun Zhou, Keyi Li, Yu Huang, Shaoyan Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vector polarimetry is an important application frontier for Rydberg-atom-based sensing. While prior research has largely concentrated on developing novel measurement schemes, high-sensitivity vector polarimetry remains an open question. Here we propose a theoretical framework for high-sensitivity detection of radio-frequency (RF) electric field polarization direction, which is particularly suitable for weak-field detection. Under a static magnetic field, the asymmetry in coupling between the Zeeman sublevels of the Rydberg atom and the RF field's polarization components enables the polarization angles to be determined from the atomic absorption index, which is retrieved via homodyne detection by incorporating the Rydberg atom system into an SU(1,1) interferometer. We derive the sensitivity of the polarization angles along with the corresponding standard quantum limit (SQL) and quantum Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound (QCRB). Our results demonstrate a sensitivity surpassing the SQL across wide angular ranges using either dual coherent states or a coherent state combined with a squeezed vacuum state as input. Significantly, the optimal sensitivity reaches below {\degree}, with sensitivities better than {\degree} maintained over most of the angular domain. This work establishes a foundation for high-precision vector polarimetry, thereby advancing the development of Rydberg-atom-based quantum sensing and contributing to a deeper understanding of light--matter interactions.

title: Quantum Frequency Comb With Pump-selectable Bin Pairing And Extraction-aware Loading In A Lithium Niobate Microresonator
authors: Mohamad Reza Nurrahman (department Of Physics, Korea Advanced Institute Of Science And Technology, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Hyeon Hwang (department Of Physics, Korea Advanced Institute Of Science And Technology, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Nuri Han (department Of Physics, Korea Advanced Institute Of Science And Technology, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Guhwan Kim (quantum Optics Research Section, Electronics And Telecommunications Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Hong-Seok Kim (quantum Optics Research Section, Electronics And Telecommunications Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Kiwon Moon (quantum Optics Research Section, Electronics And Telecommunications Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Jung Jin Ju (quantum Optics Research Section, Electronics And Telecommunications Research Institute, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Hansuek Lee (department Of Physics, Korea Advanced Institute Of Science And Technology, Daejeon, Republic Of Korea), Min-Kyo Seo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated quantum photonics requires bright, high-fidelity photon-pair sources capable of spectral multiplexing, correlation control, and circuit-compatible extraction. Cavity-enhanced spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enhances pair generation, but triply resonant operation imposes stringent pump-signal-idler spectral-alignment constraints. Moreover, the trade-off between intrinsic generation and coincidence-to-accidental ratio (CAR) does not capture the usable output flux, which depends on photon extraction. Here, we demonstrate a single-pass-pumped, resonator-enhanced quantum frequency comb (QFC) source based on a periodically poled lithium niobate photonic-crystal Fabry-P[MATH]rot microresonator. The device yields intrinsic and loaded brightnesses of 69.9 and 1.88 MHz/[MATH]W, respectively, and a maximum CAR of 16,000. Frequency-resolved measurements reveal 461 cavity-defined bins spanning 1495-1570 nm, and loaded spectral brightness approaching 4.29[MATH]10[MATH] pairs/(s[MATH]mW[MATH]nm). In particular, tuning the single-pass pump deterministically selects correlated frequency-bin pairings within the fixed QFC grid while preserving brightness and pairwise coincidence rates. We further separate intrinsic generation from output photon-pair flux, revealing the loaded-brightness-CAR relation. Together, pump-selectable bin pairing and extraction-aware loading point to tailored SPDC QFCs as chip-integrated nonclassical light resources for multiphoton-interference quantum simulation and programmable frequency-bin quantum information processing.

title: On The Generic Structures Of The Protocols For Quantum Auction And Quantum Summation And Their Relation
authors: Kabir Sandhu, Sandeep Mishra, Anirban Pathak
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Secure multi-party computation (SMC) addresses the problem of jointly computing global functions of private inputs while revealing minimal information about individual data. Two prominent examples of SMC tasks are sealed-bid auction and secure multi-party summation. Existing schemes for quantum auction and quantum summation have largely been developed independently, motivated by distinct applications and employing different computational primitives. In this work, structural symmetries in existing protocols for quantum auction and quantum summation are identified. In particular, it is established that the core auction primitives including revenue estimation, maximum bid identification, and winner determination can be reduced to repeated invocations of a summation oracle acting on suitably defined indicator functions. Conversely, summation protocols can be naturally embedded as auxiliary subroutines within auction frameworks, establishing summation as a unifying primitive underlying a broad class of auction mechanisms. Further, computational, communication and memory costs of these reductions are analyzed and compared with some of the representative existing protocols. The analysis has revealed that the process of implementing summation tasks through currently known auction protocols leads to additional overhead associated with bid-space exploration and winner determination. The proposed framework is protocol-agnostic and applicable across diverse computational models, including gate-based and photonic implementations. Finally, a proof-of-concept experimental realization (numerical validation) of a two-bidder sealed-bid auction using IBM (optical quantum) hardware is demonstrated to establish that the claimed equivalence is not merely formal but experimentally verifiable with the available hardware.

title: Detector-Conditioned Source-Space Nulls And Null-Mask Loss In A Programmable Two-Slit Interferometer
authors: Jianming Wen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Afshar's double-slit experiment probes wave--particle complementarity by placing a wire grid at the dark fringes of a downstream interference pattern while retaining an imaging basis that appears to preserve which-path information. Here we propose and analyze a time-reversed Young--Afshar configuration in which the corresponding null test is transferred from the downstream field plane to the source-label plane of a time-reversed Young interferometer. In this reciprocal geometry, a point-addressable source illuminates a double slit, while the detector remains fixed. The observed fringe is therefore not a single-shot spatial intensity pattern, but a detector-conditioned response reconstructed by scanning the source coordinate. Consequently, a null in this pattern is not a node of a freely propagating field; it is a source label for which the coherent two-slit transfer amplitude to the selected detector vanishes. A mask placed at such source-plane labels is invisible to that detector when both slits are open, yet becomes visible when either slit is opened alone. We develop the scalar Fresnel model, derive the source-space null condition, introduce a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, and examine how this loss evolves under a tunable which-path marker. The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation, so no violation of complementarity is implied. The essential new feature is instead a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity: Afshar's field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency in a reconstructed source basis.

motivation: To explore wave-particle complementarity in a reciprocal interferometer setup and clarify that no violation of complementarity occurs.
method: Develops a scalar Fresnel model, derives source-space null conditions, and introduces a detector-conditioned null-mask loss, analyzing its evolution under a tunable which-path marker.
result: The source-space visibility and path distinguishability satisfy the standard duality relation; the new feature is a reciprocal, detector-conditioned form of complementarity.
conclusion: The setup does not violate complementarity but demonstrates a reciprocal version where field-space transparency is replaced by response-function transparency.

title: Quantum LiDAR With Non-local Modulation
authors: Xiao-Dong Fan, Zhong-Hua Ou, Yun-Ru Fan, Kai Guo, Zong-Liang Xie, Qiang Qi, Li-Xun Zhang, Si Shen, Hai-Zhi Song, Yan-Yu Wei, Hao Li, Li-Xing You, Qi Zhang, Yong Liu, Guang-Can Guo, Qiang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum light detection and ranging (LiDAR) utilizes quantum entanglement and correlation to improve precision, noise resilience and covertness of target detection. Despite recent advances, the development of a quantum LiDAR system that simultaneously achieves high precision and a large measurement range remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate a quantum amplitude-modulated continuous wave LiDAR with micrometer precision achievable via increased acquisition time and meter-scale measurement range. In our demonstration, the signal photons directly illuminate the target, while the idler photons are non-locally modulated with a high-frequency cosine wave and never interact with the target. By leveraging the non-local modulation and the quantum correlation, the target detection is achieved with a precision of 0.64 [MATH] 0.06 mm within one second over a measurement range of 2-8 m. As the acquisition time is up to 500 s, the system achieves a precision of 29 [MATH]. Furthermore, our system realizes a 50 times precision improvement over the classical single-photon scheme in a background noise 37 dB stronger than the returned probe photons. With these advantages, our method will open venues for the development of high-precision, long-range, and noise-resilient target detection.

result: Achieves 0.64 mm precision over 2-8 m range in 1 second, and 29 µm precision over 500 s; 50× precision improvement over classical single-photon scheme under strong background noise.

title: Hard-core Bosons In Action: Applications To Quantum Circuits
authors: Michael Epping David Emmanuel-Costa
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of algebraic frameworks based on complex Clifford algebras for the representation and simulation of quantum circuits has been discussed in the literature. Recently, an alternative algebraic approach employing hard-core bosons has been proposed. Hard-core bosons provide a natural representation of multi-qubit systems, in which the tensor-product structure is realized directly and no sign corrections are required, in contrast to realizations based on complex Clifford algebras. Although both approaches are formally equivalent, the hard-core boson formulation exhibits computational advantages. This work reviews and extends the hard-core boson algebra for circuit simulation and presents an efficient implementation. A performance comparison with IBM Qiskit shows substantially improved execution times for simulations. Moreover, a new application is introduced in which the hard-core boson formalism is combined with genetic algorithms for quantum circuit synthesis.

conclusion: The hard-core boson formalism is a promising tool for quantum circuit simulation and synthesis, with potential for further applications.

title: Quantum Multi-Party Threshold Private Set Intersection With Explicit Cardinality Testing
authors: Zixian Gong, Kun Tian, Yi Zhang, Fengxia Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27996v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Threshold private set intersection (TPSI) allows parties to reveal their intersection only when its cardinality reaches a prescribed threshold. Existing quantum TPSI protocols typically rely on a third party (TP) to interpret the final results, which deviates from the cardinality-testing paradigm of TPSI. In this paper, we propose a quantum multiparty TPSI protocol with explicit cardinality testing. Our protocol develops a rotation-based quantum construction in which single-photon sequences are sequentially processed through participant-side data rotations, TP--participant masking rotations, and correlated aggregate rotations. This design produces hidden-label measurement vectors: TP can complete the final measurement, but cannot interpret the semantic meaning of the outcomes. Based on these hidden measurements, we further realize the threshold decision through an oblivious linear evaluation (OLE)-based inner product procedure and a lightweight garbled circuit, revealing only \(\mathbf 1[|\bigcap_i X_i|\ge \tau]\) before conditional intersection reconstruction. We prove the correctness and security of the proposed protocol, and further validate its feasibility through quantum-circuit simulations implemented on the IBM platform.
tldr: A quantum multi-party threshold private set intersection protocol with explicit cardinality testing using rotation-based encoding and oblivious linear evaluation.
motivation: Existing quantum TPSI protocols rely on a third party to interpret results, deviating from the cardinality-testing paradigm; this work aims to provide explicit threshold testing without revealing semantic meaning.
method: The protocol uses single-photon sequences with participant-side data rotations, TP-participant masking rotations, and correlated aggregate rotations to produce hidden-label measurement vectors, then applies OLE-based inner product and garbled circuits for threshold decision.
result: The protocol is proven correct and secure, and its feasibility is validated via quantum-circuit simulations on IBM's platform.
conclusion: The proposed protocol achieves explicit cardinality testing in a multi-party setting without revealing the intersection size beyond the threshold, advancing quantum private set intersection.

title: Quantum Typicality Survives non-Abelian Gauge Constraints: Exact Analytical Prediction Confirmed In $su(2)$ Lattice Gauge Theory
authors: Samuel L. Braunstein Zhi-Wei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27402v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Arguments for emergent spacetime require that quantum typicality, the generic absence of inter-subsystem correlations, persists on the physical Hilbert space of a gauge theory, where non-Abelian constraints could in principle inject geometry-supporting entanglement. Using [MATH] lattice gauge theory on two-dimensional tori ([MATH] up to [MATH]), we show that it does: the typical mutual information between strictly disjoint links matches an exact parameter-free analytical prediction combining a microcanonical baseline with Haar-random fluctuations. The Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian generates correlations from states of definite geometry (such as the electric vacuum), while generic states show only regression to the mean, establishing that the arrow of correlation growth requires a non-generic initial condition.
tldr: Quantum typicality, the absence of inter-subsystem correlations, is shown to persist in non-Abelian lattice gauge theory, with mutual information matching an analytical prediction.
motivation: To understand whether gauge constraints in non-Abelian theories can generate entanglement that supports emergent spacetime, contrary to typicality.
method: Analytical calculation of mutual information in SU(2) lattice gauge theory on tori, compared with exact diagonalization for small lattices.
result: Typical mutual information between disjoint links follows a microcanonical baseline plus Haar-random fluctuations, with no significant entanglement from gauge constraints.
conclusion: Quantum typicality survives non-Abelian gauge constraints, and correlation growth requires non-generic initial conditions.

The authors argue that emergent spacetime scenarios rely on typicality to avoid geometry-supporting entanglement from gauge constraints. Using exact diagonalization for Hilbert space dimensions up to 4,193, they compute mutual information between strictly disjoint links (separated by at least one lattice spacing) for random states drawn from the physical Hilbert space. They find that the typical mutual information matches an analytical prediction combining a microcanonical baseline (the average over all states) with Haar-random fluctuations. The Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian generates correlations from states of definite geometry (e.g., the electric vacuum), but generic states show only regression to the mean, implying that correlation growth requires a non-generic initial condition. The results support the persistence of typicality in gauge theories, with implications for emergent spacetime and the arrow of time.

title: Fault Tolerant Computation Of The Static Structure Factor And Finite Size Effects
authors: Rishabh Bhardwaj, Alexander Reed Mu\~noz, Travis E. Jones, John Golden
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27734v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum algorithms offer a promising pathway for estimating the ground-state energies of periodic materials that are beyond the practical reach of classical electronic-structure methods. A remaining challenge is finite-size mitigation: quantum algorithms evaluate a finite supercell or finite Brillouin-zone mesh, while materials properties are defined in the thermodynamic limit. In this work we develop a quantum post-processing strategy for the leading two-body finite-size correction. After one-body shell effects are reduced by twist averaging, the dominant residual error is controlled by long-wavelength density fluctuations, which are encoded in the small-momentum static structure factor [MATH]. We formulate the corresponding operator in a Bloch-orbital basis, construct its block encoding through the density operator, and estimate its ground-state expectation value using an amplified Hadamard test. We also introduce adaptive global and local binary search procedures for identifying the infrared fitting window used to reconstruct the two-body finite size error correction. The resulting cost remains subleading relative to the main ground-state energy estimation routine: the structure-factor correction has leading [MATH] dependence on the Bloch-orbital basis size, avoids the large plane-wave prefactor of full Hamiltonian simulation, and requires only [MATH] logical qubits. This provides a fault-tolerant alternative to down-sampling, replacing repeated energy calculations on larger cells with targeted measurements of the infrared density correlations that control the finite-size effects.

motivation: Quantum algorithms for ground-state energy estimation of periodic materials suffer from finite-size effects; the thermodynamic limit requires corrections that are costly to compute classically.
method: The authors formulate the static structure factor operator in a Bloch-orbital basis, construct its block encoding via the density operator, and estimate its expectation value using an amplified Hadamard test with adaptive binary search for the infrared fitting window.
result: The cost of the structure-factor correction scales sublinearly relative to the main energy estimation routine, with O(N^2) dependence on basis size and O(log N) logical qubits, avoiding large plane-wave prefactors.
conclusion: This provides a fault-tolerant alternative to down-sampling for finite-size mitigation, replacing repeated energy calculations on larger cells with targeted measurements of infrared density correlations.

title: Bottleneck Effects And Harmonic-Type Velocity Bounds For Periodic Quantum Walks
authors: Houssam Abdul-Rahman, Thomas A. Jackson, Darren C. Ong
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove explicit upper bounds on the propagation velocity of one-dimensional quantum walks with periodic coins of arbitrary period. We treat two complementary settings. First, in a perturbative regime where one transmission parameter is small, we show that the corresponding almost reflecting coin acts as a bottleneck for transport: the velocity is bounded linearly in this parameter, with an explicit leading order estimate. Second, for arbitrary nonzero transmission parameters, we prove a general a priori bound in terms of their harmonic mean, together with a refined version that detects the spatial variation of neighboring coins. Moreover, we prove a general lower bound on the velocity. These bounds apply directly to the corresponding CMV setting.
tldr: Proves velocity bounds for periodic quantum walks using bottleneck and harmonic mean arguments.
motivation: Understand transport limits in quantum walks with periodic coins, relevant to quantum information propagation.
method: Analytical bounds derived from transmission parameters and harmonic means, applied to CMV matrices.
result: Explicit upper and lower bounds on propagation velocity, including linear scaling for small transmission.
conclusion: Periodic quantum walks have velocity constraints determined by coin parameters, with potential implications for quantum transport.

Additionally, a general lower bound on the velocity is provided. The results are directly applicable to the corresponding CMV (Cantero-Moral-Velázquez) setting, which is a unitary representation of orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle.

title: End-to-End Learning Of Quantum Control On Latent Dynamical Manifold
authors: Jun-Dong Zhong, Zong-Yuan Ge, Feng-Hua Ren, Zhao-Ming Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional quantum control relies on an iterative "simulate-then-optimize" paradigm, where dynamics simulation and control design are decoupled, leading to substantial computational overhead and limited scalability, particularly in noisy environments. Here, we propose an end-to-end quantum control framework based on long short-term memory, in which system dynamics and control strategies are learned jointly in a low dimensional latent manifold. The model directly maps initial states and environmental parameters to both dynamical trajectories and optimized control pulse in a single forward pass. The framework is validated on adiabatic speedup in a two-level system and state transfer in a one-dimensional spin chain under noise, achieving accurate dynamical prediction and control optimization. It improves the fidelity for both tasks and significantly reduces the optimization cost by three orders of magnitude compared with conventional iterative methods, while exhibiting strong generalization to multi-parameter, time-varying noise, as well as to different initial states and driving fields. Our work introduces a data-driven control paradigm based on latent manifold learning, reducing the computational bottleneck of iterative optimization and enabling real-time adaptive control of complex open quantum systems.
tldr: An end-to-end deep learning framework for quantum control that jointly learns dynamics and control in a latent manifold, achieving faster optimization and robustness to noise.
motivation: Traditional quantum control methods are computationally expensive and decouple simulation from optimization, limiting scalability and real-time adaptability.
method: The authors use a long short-term memory (LSTM) network to map initial states and noise parameters directly to dynamical trajectories and control pulses, learning a low-dimensional latent representation of the system.
result: The method achieves accurate prediction and control optimization, improving fidelity and reducing optimization cost by three orders of magnitude compared to iterative methods, with strong generalization to time-varying noise and different initial states.
conclusion: This data-driven approach offers a scalable and real-time alternative for quantum control, particularly in noisy open quantum systems.

title: Survivor-conditioned Renewal Laws And Observable Bounds For Open Intermittent Maps
authors: Jason Duvall
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent numerical computations and stochastic modeling by Brevitt and Klages suggest that introducing a hole in a Pomeau--Manneville map can suppress survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching. We prove a deterministic renewal theorem which explains this phenomenon and its observable-level generalizations. For an open intermittent map induced on a base away from the neutral fixed point, we describe the asymptotic distribution of the number of completed survivor returns to the base, conditioned on survival up to time [MATH]. The limiting law is expressed in terms of the killed induced transfer operator; for the conditionally invariant density of the killed induced system it is geometric. We then prove two reward results for additive observables. A reward domination theorem gives bounded survivor-conditioned Birkhoff sums, while a stronger final-tail asymptotic gives convergence to a finite limit. For generalized Pomeau--Manneville maps, bounded observables satisfying [MATH] near the neutral fixed point and a mild variation condition satisfy the domination hypotheses. When the neutral branch and final tails satisfy the corresponding regularity assumptions, asymptotically regular observables satisfy the convergence hypotheses. In particular, [MATH] gives bounded survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching for the generalized class; under these additional regularity assumptions, it converges. Under an additional entropy-domination assumption, we also derive a zero entropy-rate consequence for survivor return-length names and record the complementary linear growth of stretching when the hole contains a neighborhood of the neutral fixed point.
tldr: Proves renewal laws and observable bounds for open intermittent maps, focusing on survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching.
motivation: To explain numerical observations of suppressed Lyapunov stretching in Pomeau-Manneville maps with holes.
method: Uses deterministic renewal theory and killed induced transfer operators to derive asymptotic distributions and reward results.
result: Establishes a renewal theorem, reward domination, and final-tail convergence for bounded observables under regularity conditions.
conclusion: Provides rigorous justification for the suppression of survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching and generalizes to other observables.

The authors prove a deterministic renewal theorem that explains this suppression and its generalizations to other observables. They consider an open intermittent map induced on a base away from the neutral fixed point and describe the asymptotic distribution of the number of completed survivor returns to the base, conditioned on survival up to time t. The limiting law is expressed in terms of the killed induced transfer operator; for the conditionally invariant density of the killed induced system, it is geometric. Two reward results for additive observables are then proved: a reward domination theorem giving bounded survivor-conditioned Birkhoff sums, and a stronger final-tail asymptotic giving convergence to a finite limit. For generalized Pomeau–Manneville maps, bounded observables satisfying |ψ(x)| ≤ C x^γ near the neutral fixed point and a mild variation condition satisfy the domination hypotheses. When the neutral branch and final tails satisfy corresponding regularity assumptions, asymptotically regular observables satisfy the convergence hypotheses. In particular, ψ = log|f'| gives bounded survivor-conditioned Lyapunov stretching for the generalized class; under additional regularity assumptions, it converges. Under an entropy-domination assumption, a zero entropy-rate consequence for survivor return-length names is derived, and complementary linear growth of stretching when the hole contains a neighborhood of the neutral fixed point is recorded.

The reward results are obtained via martingale approximations and coupling arguments, exploiting the renewal structure. title: Multi-parameter Two-photon Polarimetry At The Quantum Limit
authors: Joseph Niblo, Luca Maggio, Russell M. J. Brooks, Joseph Ho, Vincenzo Tamma, Alessandro Fedrizzi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic quantum metrology has demonstrated advantages in precision and resource efficiency for a wide range of applications, with several schemes approaching the fundamental quantum Cram\'er-Rao precision bound (QCRB). However, the intrinsic incompatibility of quantum measurements represents a hurdle in extending these advantages to the simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters. In this paper, we present an experimental protocol approaching the QCRB simultaneously in two polarisation parameters, across a wide range of the parameter space, with as few as [MATH] photon pairs, offering advantages for polarimetric sensing for dim sources such as in X-ray astronomy or photosensitive samples.
tldr: Experimental demonstration of multi-parameter two-photon polarimetry approaching the quantum Cramér-Rao bound.
motivation: Extend quantum metrology advantages to simultaneous estimation of multiple polarization parameters, relevant for dim sources like X-ray astronomy.
method: Uses entangled photon pairs and a tailored measurement protocol to achieve near-optimal precision for two polarization parameters.
result: Approaches the quantum Cramér-Rao bound simultaneously for both parameters across a wide parameter range with few photon pairs.
conclusion: Demonstrates practical multi-parameter quantum polarimetry at the quantum limit, with potential applications in low-light polarimetric sensing.

title: Universal Framework For The Design Of Near-zero Refractive Index Photonic Crystals
authors: Micha\"el Lobet Adrien Debacq
